title: 46 Exploring the immune enhancing potential of Spirulina platensis and its impact on gut microbial diversity in laying hens
content:
Abstract
Spirulina platensis (SP), a nutrient-dense cyanobacterium, is gaining attention as an eco-friendly dietary supplement in livestock nutrition due to its immune-enhancing and health-promoting properties. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of SP on immune markers and gut microbial diversity in laying hens. A total of 192 White Leghorn hens (39 weeks old, 1670 ± 66 g) were randomly assigned to four dietary groups: 0 g/kg (control), 2.5 g/kg, 5 g/kg, and 10 g/kg SP supplementation for six weeks. Each group consisted eight replicates, with six birds per replicate. At the end of the experiment, blood samples were collected from two birds per replicate through the wing vein to determine serum levels of interleukins (IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, IL-16, IL-21), vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), interferons (IFNα, IFNγ), macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF), macrophage inflammatory proteins (MIP-1b, MIP-3a), and RANTES. Moreover, fecal samples from one chicken per replicate (eight samples per group) were collected and genomic DNA was extracted for 16S rRNA sequencing to evaluate microbial diversity and composition. Data analysis was performed using a completely randomized design with SAS 9.4 software. Statistical analysis involved one-way ANOVA to evaluate the effects of dietary treatments, followed by Duncan’s multiple range test for mean comparisons. Orthogonal polynomial contrasts were used to assess linear and quadratic responses to increasing levels of SP supplementation. The results showed a dose-dependent improvement in several immune markers. IL-16 and IL-10 levels increased linearly (P< 0.05) in the SP groups (2.5, 5, and 10 g/kg) compared to the control, with the highest levels observed at 10 g/kg. Similarly, MIP-1b, M-CSF, and RANTES levels increased significantly (P< 0.05), while MIP-3a levels decreased linearly (P< 0.05) and quadratically (P< 0.05), indicating enhanced immune function and reduced inflammation. VEGF and interferon levels (IFNα, IFNγ) also showed significant improvements, particularly at higher SP supplementation levels. Microbial analysis revealed changes in gut microbiota composition. Firmicutes increased across treatments, highest at 10 g/kg SP group, with genera within this phylum dominating compared to other groups. Actinobacteriota was most abundant at 2.5 g/kg SP, with related genera also more prevalent. Bacteroidota was consistently lower in all treatments than in the control, both at the phylum and genus levels. Desulfobacterota peaked at 5 g/kg SP, while Proteobacteria and their associated genera were highest at 2.5 g/kg SP. Alpha diversity indices (Chao1, Shannon, Simpson) showed no significant (P >0.05) differences between control and SP groups. NMDS analysis based on UniFrac distances revealed distinct microbial clustering in the control group, with overlapping clusters among the treatment groups, indicating similar community structures within treatments. These findings indicate the potential of SP as a dietary supplement to enhance immunity, reduce inflammation, and modulate gut microbiota in laying hens.
